This effect depends on three key factors: the asteroid's physical shape, the magnitude and distribution of solar heating, and the resulting thermal inertia. Because these characteristics vary between bodies, researchers typically employ a scale-invariant approach, expressing the YORP acceleration as $\text{YORP} \propto a^{-3}$ to isolate its geometric dependence. While widely adopted, assuming this pure scaling for all small asteroids is likely incorrect. A representative case involves the asteroid 2002 AT4, composed of two primary fragments and several smaller attached bodies. Our findings indicate that while a geometrically similar solid of the same total mass rotating at different distances would exhibit varying YORP effects purely due to scale, 2002 AT4 displays distinct thermal and geometric irregularities causing rotational YORP accelerations that range from approximately 30% lower to 30% higher than expected via simple scaling laws.
